title: Men's T-Shirt Sewing Pattern – Free PDF
content:
Garment Men's crew neck T-shirt

Level Easy

Sizes 35 – 52 (XS – 2XL)

Fabric Cotton jersey, cotton-elastane, slub or cotton-modal jersey, with cotton rib

Pieces 5

This free men's T-shirt sewing pattern is the plain crew neck tee you reach for every morning: a straight, easy fit, short set-in sleeves and a neat rib neckband, with matching rib cuffs on the sleeves. It is quick to cut, quick to sew, and a lovely way to get comfortable with knit fabrics if you have only sewn wovens so far.

→ Jump to the free download

1 cm (3/8″) seam allowance included on all pieces · 2 cm (3/4″) body hem · neckband cut from rib to the size table

Design details of the men's crew neck T-shirt

Think of the tee you would buy in a good basics shop, then make it fit you better. The body is cut straight from the chest to a slightly curved hem, with about 6 to 7 cm of ease at the chest, so it sits close without clinging. The sleeves end halfway down the upper arm and finish in a folded rib cuff, which gives the tee a slightly more finished, vintage look than a plain turned-up hem.

Reading the sketch

On the front, the double dashed lines around the neck show the twin-needle topstitching that holds the neckband seam flat. The small vertical lines at the end of each sleeve are the ribs of the cuff. There are no other lines on the body: no pocket, no centre seam, no darts.

The back is just as simple, with the neckband visible across the back neck and the same rib cuffs on the sleeves. The hem curves gently down at the sides and up at the centre, which is why the tee looks clean worn untucked.

  • Round crew neckline with a folded rib neckband, 2.5 cm (1″) finished, topstitched with a twin needle
  • Short set-in sleeves, sewn flat before the side seams for an easier first knit project
  • Folded rib cuffs, about 2 cm (3/4″) wide
  • Front and back each cut in one piece, on a single layer, no centre seams
  • Slightly curved hem, turned up 2 cm and stitched with a twin needle or a zigzag

If you have never sewn jersey before, this is the pattern to start with. Every seam is short and straight, the sleeves go in flat, and the neckband is the only step where you need to stretch a piece evenly. Once that clicks, you can make a new tee in an evening.

Sizing guide

Measure your chest around the fullest part, keeping the tape level under the arms, and pick the size from the table. The chest decides the size of a T-shirt: waist and hip are only there as a guide. If you are between two sizes, take the larger one for a slightly more relaxed fit. Not sure how to measure? See how to take body measurements and how to choose your pattern size.

Men's sizes 35 to 52 (the size is the chest in inches), drafted for a height of 180 cm (5 ft 11 in). Letter sizes are a guide only: 35 = XS · 36–37 = S · 38–40 = M · 42–44 = L · 46–48 = XL · 50–52 = 2XL. Always choose by measurements.

Body measurements

Finished T-shirt measurements

There is about 6 to 7 cm (2½″) of ease at the chest. Sleeve length is measured from the shoulder point to the cuff edge, cuff included; back length from the neckline seam to the hem at the centre back.

Fabric amounts

Estimated with every piece laid on a single layer, grain lines parallel to the selvedge so the stretch goes around the body, plus about 8 % for shrinkage and straightening. The rib should be at least 60 cm (24″) wide or tubular. Buy a little more for stripes, and pre-wash the jersey and the rib before cutting.

Common fit adjustments

Length. The tee is drafted for 180 cm. To lengthen or shorten it, cut the front and back across halfway between the armhole and the hem, spread or overlap the same amount on both pieces and redraw the side seams. Full guide: how to lengthen or shorten a sewing pattern.

Neckband too loose or too tight. Rib varies a lot. A very stretchy rib can be cut 1 to 2 cm shorter than the table, a firm one 1 to 2 cm longer. Pin it on before you sew: it should lie flat around the neckline without puckers.

Materials

  • Main fabric: 0.9 to 2.0 m (1 to 2 1/4 yd) of single cotton jersey with 20 to 30 % stretch across the width and good recovery, about 160 to 220 g/m²
  • Rib: 0.25 m (3/8 yd) of 1x1 or 2x2 cotton rib for the neckband and cuffs, matching or contrast
  • Thread: polyester all-purpose thread (and overlocker thread if you use one)
  • Needles: ballpoint or stretch needle 75 to 90, and a 4 mm twin stretch needle (optional)
  • Optional: 1 cm (3/8 in) knit stay tape or clear elastic for the shoulder seams
  • Pins or clips, chalk or a washable marker

Pattern pieces

  • 1 Front: cut 1 on a single layer, right side up (drawn whole)
  • 2 Back: cut 1 on a single layer, right side up (drawn whole)
  • 3 Sleeve: cut 2, flipping the piece over for the second one
  • 4 Sleeve cuff: cut 2 in rib, stretch along the cuff length
  • 5 Neckband: cut 1 in rib, 6 cm (2 3/8″) wide, length from the table (not printed)

Neckband length per size

Cut the band 6 cm (2 3/8″) wide with the stretch going along the length. The length is about 85 % of the neckline plus 1 cm at each end for the joining seam.

Choosing fabric for a T-shirt

A good tee starts with a good jersey. Look for a single cotton jersey that stretches 20 to 30 % across the width and springs back when you let go: around 160 to 220 g/m² is the sweet spot, light enough to feel soft and heavy enough not to show every seam. Cotton with a little elastane holds its shape longer, slub jersey gives a relaxed weekend texture and cotton-modal feels silky and drapes well.

For the neckband and cuffs, use a 1x1 or 2x2 cotton rib with good recovery. Matching rib gives a classic basic; a contrast colour looks sporty and vintage. Avoid very thin, slippery or loose knits for your first try, because they make the neckband harder to sew neatly. More tips in our guides on how to choose fabric for sewing patterns and how to sew stretch fabrics.

Sewing notes

Fit and style

A straight, regular fit with a little ease at the chest. Cut your usual size first, then go up a size next time if you prefer a roomier tee.

Fabric

Knits only: the tee relies on stretch to go over the head. Use a ballpoint needle and let the feed dogs move the jersey, never pull it.

Stitches

A narrow zigzag (width 0.5 to 1, length 2.5) or a stretch stitch for the seams. See how to sew stretch fabrics.

Get the pattern

Free PDF pattern, one file per size, men's sizes 35 to 52 (XS to 2XL). Share your make with #sewcraftly!

Download A4
Download US Letter

Print page 1 at 100% and check that the test square measures 10 cm (4 in). New to PDF patterns? Read how to print and assemble a PDF pattern.

Sewing steps

Seam allowance 1 cm (3/8″) unless stated otherwise. Sew right sides together with an overlocker, a narrow zigzag or a stretch stitch, and press every seam before it is crossed by another one.

  1. Shoulders. Pin the front to the back at the shoulders, right sides together. Add a strip of stay tape or clear elastic to the back shoulder if you like, then stitch, finish and press toward the back.
  2. Neckband. Join the short ends of the band, fold it in half lengthwise and divide it into quarters. Pin it to the neckline with the seam at the centre back, matching the quarter marks to the centre front and the shoulders, then stitch with the band on top, stretching the band and never the neckline. Press the seam toward the body and topstitch with a twin needle or a narrow zigzag.
  3. Sleeves, sewn flat. Pin each sleeve to its armhole: single notch to the front, double notch to the back, top notch to the shoulder seam. Spread the small ease of the cap evenly and stitch with the sleeve underneath.
  4. Side and sleeve seams. Fold the tee right sides together and sew from the end of the sleeve to the hem in one continuous seam, matching the underarm seams and the side notches.
  5. Rib cuffs. Close each cuff into a loop, fold it in half lengthwise and slip it over the right side of the sleeve, seam at the underarm. Stretch the cuff to fit as you stitch through all three layers, then press toward the sleeve.
  6. Hem. Turn up 2 cm (3/4″), press and stitch about 1.5 cm from the fold with a twin needle, or with a zigzag from the wrong side. Give the whole tee a final steam press and let it cool flat.

Tips and common mistakes

A wavy neckline. It almost always comes from stretching the neckline instead of the band. Keep the T-shirt relaxed under the band, stretch only the rib between the pins, and steam the seam: a slight wave settles once pressed.

Skipped stitches. Change to a fresh ballpoint or stretch needle. A universal needle can pierce the knit loops and skip, especially on cotton-elastane.

A hem that tunnels. A ridge between twin-needle rows means the bobbin tension is too tight or the fabric was pulled. Loosen the upper tension slightly and use a strip of wash-away tape or a lighter press foot pressure.

Cuffs that twist. Cut the rib with the stretch going along the length of the cuff and match the cuff seam to the underarm seam before you pin the rest.

How to style a men's crew neck T-shirt

Everyday basic: white, heather grey or navy jersey under an open overshirt or a denim jacket.

Smart casual: a heavier, plain jersey tucked into chinos with a leather belt and clean sneakers.

Weekend: a slub jersey with contrast rib, worn loose over shorts. The tee also pairs nicely with our free men's chino shorts sewing pattern.

Want to build a small handmade wardrobe? Add a button-up from our free men's shirt sewing pattern and wear it open over the tee.

Care

Wash at 30 °C (cold) inside out with similar colours, and dry flat or tumble dry low. Iron on the wrong side at medium heat, without stretching the neckline.

Questions

Is seam allowance included?

Yes: 1 cm (3/8″) on every edge, including the neckline, the cuffs and the neckband, plus a 2 cm (3/4″) hem on the body.

Which paper sizes are included?

The free download has A4 and US Letter files, one file per size, so you only print the size you need.

Which size should I choose?

Choose by your chest measurement in the size chart, not by your shop size. Between two sizes, take the larger one for a more relaxed tee.

Is this T-shirt pattern good for a beginner?

Yes. It has five pieces and no closures, so it is a great first knit project. The neckband is the only step that needs a little patience.

Do I need an overlocker?

No. A narrow zigzag or the stretch stitch of a normal sewing machine works for every seam. A twin needle gives a neat finish on the neckline, cuffs and hem, but a zigzag works too.

What fabric works best for a men's T-shirt?

A single cotton jersey with 20 to 30 % stretch across the width, about 160 to 220 g/m². Cotton-elastane, slub jersey and cotton-modal jersey also work, with a cotton rib for the neckband and cuffs.

Why is the neckband not on the pattern sheet?

It is a simple rectangle, so you cut it from rib using the length table for your size: 6 cm wide and about 85 % of the neckline length.

Can I make it longer or shorter?

Yes. The pattern is drafted for a height of 180 cm. Cut the front and back across halfway between the armhole and the hem, spread or overlap the same amount on both, and redraw the side seams.
